rows.verified: Health surveillance is a programme of repeated checks intended to identify ill health caused by work.
Health surveillance is required where workers remain exposed to relevant health risks after suitable controls have been applied.
Noise, vibration and hazardous-substance exposure are examples of risks that can trigger health-surveillance duties.
A health-surveillance scheme should normally be designed with input from a competent occupational-health professional.
Certain hazards, including asbestos, lead and ionising radiation, can require medical surveillance under specific legal regimes.
Where an appointed doctor is legally required, the employer must use a competent occupational-health doctor appointed by HSE, subject to limited exceptions.
Health surveillance is distinct from general health screening, health promotion and non-work-related wellbeing checks.
Surveillance findings should feed back into the risk assessment, control measures, worker information and training.
The need and method for health surveillance depend on the identifiable health effect, residual exposure, valid detection techniques and the work population.
Health-surveillance evidence is exposure-, worker-, hazard- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
Employers have the same core health, safety and welfare responsibilities for workers under 18 as for other workers.
Young people may face increased risk when new to work because they can be less familiar with workplace hazards and controls.
Risk assessment should consider limited experience, lack of maturity, physical development and awareness of existing or potential risks.
An employer should review the risk assessment before employing a young person for the first time or where particular needs exist.
Young workers need clear and sufficient instruction, training and supervision proportionate to the work risk.
Employers should check that young workers understand workplace hazards, precautions and the training provided.
Young people may need closer supervision and additional support compared with experienced adult workers.
Work-experience students are treated as employees for workplace health-and-safety purposes, with the placement employer holding the main duty.
Young-worker controls depend on age, maturity, capability, task, equipment, work environment and supervision quality.
Young-worker guidance is person-, task-, equipment- and placement-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
